Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 80, verse 1–3:

﴿He frowned and turned away﴾ meaning: he frowned in the face of the blind man and turned away from him. Ibn 'Atiyya said: addressing him in the third person is an intensification of the reproach, since it contains a degree of turning away. Al-Zamakhshari said: reporting it in the third person adds to the disapproval. Others said it is an honouring of the Prophet (ﷺ) and an exalting of him above being addressed directly with reproach, and this is the best view. ﴿Because the blind man came to him﴾: this is in the position of a object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi), and it is in the accusative case, governed by either "tawalla" or "'abasa." Ibn Umm Maktum is mentioned with the word "the blind man" to show that his blindness is what caused him to be despised. In this there is evidence that mentioning such physical afflictions is permissible when there is a benefit in it, or when the person concerned is being identified, and among this is the saying of the scholars of hadith: Sulayman al-A'mash and 'Abd al-Rahman al-A'raj, and other such examples. ﴿And what could make you know﴾ meaning: what informs you of the condition of this blind man? ﴿Perhaps he would purify himself﴾ meaning: he would purify himself and benefit in his religion from what he hears from you.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 80, verses 5–10:

﴿As for him who thinks himself self-sufficient, / to him you attend eagerly﴾, i.e., you turn your attention to the wealthy man, hoping that he will become Muslim. ﴿And it is not your responsibility if he does not purify himself﴾, i.e., there is no blame on you if this wealthy man does not purify himself. ﴿But as for him who came to you striving [eagerly], / and in fear [of Allah]﴾, a reference to ʿAbd Allah ibn Umm Maktum. The meaning of "yasʿa" (strives) is that he hastens in his walking out of his eagerness to seek goodness. ﴿while he fears [Allah]﴾, or fears the disbelievers and their harm to him for following you. It was also said: he came with no one to lead him, so he feared that he would fall; but this view is weak. ﴿you ignore him﴾, i.e., you occupy yourself away from him with someone else, from the saying "lahiytu ʿan al-shayʾ" (I turned away from the thing) when one has abandoned it. It is narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took discipline from what Allah had disciplined him with in this surah, so afterwards he never turned away from a poor man, nor paid attention to a wealthy man. Likewise, the excellent scholars followed him, so that the poor in the assembly of Sufyan al-Thawri were like princes, and the wealthy would wish to be poor.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on Surah 80, verses 11–16:

﴿Kallā﴾ (Nay, indeed) is a rebuke against returning to what the reproach was about. ﴿Innahā tadhkiratun﴾ (Indeed, it is a reminder) has two interpretations. The first: this preceding discourse is a reminder or admonition to the Prophet ﷺ. The second: the Qur'an is a reminder for all people, so no one should be given preference over another in it. This second view is more likely (arjah), because it fits what follows: ﴿Fa-man shā'a dhakarahu﴾ (So whoever wills, let him remember it) and what comes after. The pronoun in ﴿Innahā tadhkiratun﴾ is feminine in accordance with the meaning of "story," "admonition," "surah," or "recitation." It is masculine in ﴿Fa-man shā'a dhakarahu﴾ in accordance with the meaning of "admonition" or "reminder," or the Qur'an.

﴿Fī ṣuḥufin﴾ (in scrolls) is an attribute of "reminder," meaning established in scrolls. These are the scrolls copied from the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-maḥfuẓ). It has also been said that they are the codices (maṣāḥif) of the Muslims. ﴿Marfūʿatin﴾ (exalted) : if the scrolls are the codices, the meaning is exalted in rank; if they are the scrolls of the angels, the meaning is likewise. Or it means raised up in the heavens, and ﴿muṭahharatin﴾ (purified), meaning free from the hands of the devils. ﴿Bi-aydī safaratin﴾ (in the hands of scribes): these are the angels. Safara is the plural of sāfir, meaning scribe, because they write the Qur'an. It has also been said that they are called safara because they are envoys (sufarā') between God and His servants. It has further been said that it means the reciters among people. The first view is more likely (arjah). The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "The one who is skilled in the Qur'an is with the noble, obedient scribes," meaning that he performs the same work as they do in writing and reciting the Qur'an, or that he receives a reward for the Qur'an similar to their reward.

**"Man is killed"**: a curse upon him, following the Arab custom of using this expression in invocation. Its meaning is to disparage his state and to say that he deserves to be spoken of this way. It was also said that it means "cursed," but this is a weak view.

**"How disbelieving he is!"**: an expression of wonder at the intensity of his disbelief, though he is obligated to do otherwise.

**"From what thing did He create him?"**: a question of rebuke and affirmation (*tawqif wa taqrir*). He then answers it with His words: **"From a drop of semen He created him"**, meaning *al-mani'* (seminal fluid). The purpose of the statement is to belittle man, and its meaning is that he must recognize the Lord who created him.

**"Then He made him proportionate"**: He prepared him for what suits him. From the same usage: **"And He created everything and determined it with precise determination"** [al-Furqan: 2]. It was also said that it means He made him according to a known measure in his provision, his term of life, and other matters.

**"Then the way He made easy for him"**: the word *al-sabil* ("the way") is in the accusative by a suppressed verb, which the verb *yassarahu* ("He made it easy") explains. There are three opinions about its meaning:
1. He made easy the way of his exit from his mother's womb.
2. It is the way of good and evil, based on His words: **"Indeed We guided him to the way, either grateful or ungrateful"** [al-Insan: 3].
3. It is the way of sound reflection that leads to faith.

The first is the preferred view, because it is joined to His words **"from a drop of semen He created him, then made him proportionate."** This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas.

**"Then He causes him to die and buries him"**: meaning He made him one who has a grave. One says *qabartu al-mayyit* when one buries the dead, and *aqbartuhu* when one orders that he be buried.

**"Then when He wills, He will raise him up"**: meaning He will resurrect him from his grave. One says *nashara al-mayyit* when the dead person rises, and *ansharahu Allah* when God raises him. The phrase "when He wills" refers to the Day of Resurrection, that is, the time at which He is able to raise him.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 80, verse 23–31:

﴿Nay⦆ — a rebuke to man for what he is engaged in. ﴿He has not yet fulfilled what He commanded him﴾, meaning: man, despite the length of his life, has not fulfilled what Allah commanded him. Some of them said: no one ever fulfils all that Allah has made obligatory upon him, since a servant must necessarily fall short. ﴿Then let man look at his food﴾: this is a command to reflect upon food, how Allah created it by His power and facilitated it by His mercy. Therefore it is obligatory upon the servant to obey and thank Him, and disobedience to Him and disbelief in Him are ugly. It was also said: "Let him look at his food" refers to when it becomes excrement, so that he sees the lowliness of this world and the baseness of his own self. The first is more well-known and more evident in the meaning of the verse, although the second view is sound, and see how he explained it with His saying: ﴿That We poured down the water in torrents﴾ and what follows, in order to enumerate the blessings and manifest the power. It was also read "innā ṣababnā al-mā'" with a fatḥah on the hamzah, as a substitution (badal) for "al-ṭaʿām" (food). ﴿Then We split the earth asunder﴾, meaning: plants come forth from it. ﴿Grain﴾, meaning wheat, barley and all other grains. ﴿Grapes and herbage﴾ (qaḍban): it was said this is fiṣfiṣah (clover/alfalfa), and it was said it is fodder for beasts; Ibn ʿAṭiyyah chose that it refers to vegetables and the like that are eaten fresh. ﴿Dense gardens﴾, meaning thick and lush. ﴿And fruit and pasture﴾: al-abb is the pasture according to Ibn ʿAbbās and the majority; it was also said it is chaff, and Abū Bakr (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu) hesitated in its interpretation.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 80, verse 33–40:

﴿ٱلصَّآخَّةُ﴾ The Deafening Blast: it refers to the Resurrection. It is derived from your saying: ṣakha al-udhun (ṣakhkha al-udhn), meaning the ear was deafened by a very loud cry. It may be an allusion to the blast in the Trumpet (al-ṣūr), or to the severity of the matter, such that whoever hears it is deafened by its difficulty. It has also been said that it derives from your saying: aṣākha li-l-ḥadīth (asākha), meaning he listened attentively to the speech. The first (meaning) is the one that accords with the derivation.

﴿يَوْمَ يَفِرُّ ٱلْمَرْءُ مِنْ أَخِيهِ﴾ "On the Day a man will flee from his brother" (80:34), and the verse that follows.
